p: The West India Docks opened in 1802, built by merchants to handle the huge volume of sugar, rum and coffee arriving from the Caribbean. That makes this warehouse a direct witness to the trade it explains, which is why the gallery on London, sugar and slavery hits so hard. It's worth knowing that the statue of Robert Milligan, the merchant and slave owner who drove the docks' creation, was taken down from outside the museum in 2020. The museum tackles that history head on, and older children will come away with plenty to talk about.

The museum was previously called the Museum of London Docklands and took its new name as part of the wider rebrand of the London Museum. General entry has traditionally been free, so it's a great pick if you're watching the pennies on a London trip. Allow two to three hours if you want to take in every floor, or an hour or so if you're mainly there for Sailortown and the children's gallery. Weekday mornings in term time tend to be calmer.

Getting there is easy. As well as the DLR, the Elizabeth line and the Jubilee line both stop at Canary Wharf, a short stroll away. If you fancy arriving by water, Thames Clipper river buses call at Canary Wharf pier. Make a day of it by carrying on south through the Isle of Dogs to Mudchute Farm, a proper working city farm with animals for the kids to meet, then walk under the Thames through the Greenwich foot tunnel from Island Gardens. You'll pop up beside the Cutty Sark with Greenwich's markets, park and maritime sights all waiting.
